full_judgment:
3. At the trial 11 witnesses including the complainant Tazul Islam were examined. The informant Mr. Tazul Islam, SI of Police Narshindi PS deposed as PW 1, Mainul Huq SI of Police of that PS deposed as PW 2, MA Jalil SI of Shibpur PS deposed as PW 3, Santosh Kumar Kar, the local member of Panchaduma Union Parishad deposed at PW 4, Mr. A Majid, member of Panchaduma Union Parishad deposed as PW 5, Sanaullah, the son of Fazur Ali who is alleged to have been murdered by the pipe-gun, Ext. 1, has deposed as PW 611 Constable No.193 Siddikur Rahman deposed as PW 7, constable No. 317 Hadi Sowkat deposed as PW 8, Constable No.103 Omar Ali deposed as PW 9, Constable No. 250 Abu Taher deposed as PW 10 and the Investigating Officer Mr. Tazul Islam (PW 1) also deposed as PW 11. 

 4. The learned Special Tribunal on consideration of the evidence of this witness and other circumstances on record found the accused-appellant guilty under section 19A of the Arms Act read with Special Powers Act and convicted and sentenced him as aforesaid. 

 6. The learned Advocate for the appellant has submitted that the prosecution has not been able to prove the manner, time and place of occurrence as alleged by the prosecution. He has submitted that in the charge the time of occurrence has been given as 10-00 AM but in the FIR in the charge-sheet and in the evidence of the PWs the time of recovery has been stated to be 3-30 PM. This he has submitted has prejudiced the accused in his defence. 

 7. Secondly, he has submitted that the witnesses except the PWs 4 and 5 are all police personnel and their evidence should be taken with a grain of salt. Furthermore, PWs 4 and 5 who are said to be independent witnesses are inimically disposed towards the appellant as has been revealed in their cross-examination. The learned Advocate for the appellant has further submitted that in this case the procedure under sections 25 and 29 of the Arms Act and 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure has not been complied with at the time of alleged recovery of the gur, Ext. 1. Lastly, he has submitted that the place of recovery of the gun was accessible from outside and the accused-appellant did not possess the gun with knowledge of its existence in his hut. Nor was the appellant the only owner in possession of the ghar from which the gun is said to have been recovered. He has submitted that mere recovery of the gun by the accused appellant without definite proof that he had kept the gun would not incriminate him. He has submitted that the circumstances of the case would show that the appellant had not kept the gun with intention which might form mensrea. Under these circumstance, he has submitted, the accused is entitled to acquittal and the judgment and order of conviction passed by the learned Special Tribunal are liable to be set aside. 

 9. Next, he has submitted that the evidence of all the witnesses of recovery is good and proper evidence under section 3 of the Evidence Act. All the witnesses have stood the test of cross-examination. He has submitted that the conviction of the accused-appellant can be based only upon the official witnesses but in the instant case there was evidence of two seizure-list witnesses, PWs 4 and 5, who are respectable witnesses of the locality. He has submitted that the defence could not substantiate the suggestion that these two witnesses were inimically disposed towards the accused-appellant. 

 10. The learned Advocate for the State further submitted that in the instant case the provision of sections 25 and 29 and 30 of the Arms Act and 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure are not to be complied with as it is the accused appellant himself who had recovered the gun from his own possession and there was no necessity of such search before the recovery of the gun, Lastly the learned Advocate for the State has submitted that the dwelling ghar of the accused-appellant from the top of the wall of which the gun was recovered was not accessible to the outsiders and none else has been proved to have been in occupation of the house except the accused-appellant. The learned Advocate Mr. Shah Azizur Rahman for the State has, therefore, urged that the judgment and order of conviction and sentence passed by the learned Tribunal will have to be confirmed and the appeal dismissed. 

 11. We have gone through the evidence and the Judgment in this case. PW 1 Tazul Islam who lodged the FIR has supported the FIR case in his deposition. He has stated that in course of investigation into the case No. 15 dated 24.7.84 under section 302 of the Penal Code he arrested Moyezuddin on suspicion and later he arrested the appellant Hashem Master who confessed to him of his possession of the pipe-gun, material Ext. 1. Then he went to the house of Hashem Master along with appellant Hashem Master himself, Moyezudd in and his police force as well as PWs 4 and 5 to witness the recovery of the gun at the instance of Hashem Master. He has stated that accused appellant Abul Hashem Master brought out the pipe-gun, Ext. 1 from the top of the wall of his mud-walled tin-shed of the westerr. bhiti which was 819 cubits high in presence of all witnesses. Then he prepared the seizure-list and obtained the signatures of three witnesses in the seizure-list. Thereafter, he lodged the FIR, Ext. 1. In reply to his cross-examination he has disclosed that the case into which he was investigating initially was the murder case of Fazar Ali. He arrested Moyezuddin on 26.7.84 and upon his statement he arrested appellart Abul Hashem from the house of one Abu Sayed. The appellant Abul Hashem made certain statements to PW 1. He took both Moyezuddin and Abul Hashem and other witnesses in the case to the house of accused Abul Hashem for recovery of the arms. The appellant did not disclose exactly where he kept the arms and he first searched outside of his hut but did not get anything there. Then again he started search and after 5n minutes he brought out the gun from the outside of the mud-wall with the help of forked bamboo pole. He has stated that there was a gap between the wall and the tin-shed and one could push his hand from the outside of the mud-wall. He prepared the seizure-list on the spot but he did not take the signature of accused Hashem on the seizure-list and he did not supply a copy of the seizure-list to him. He has stated that appellant Hashem brought out the gun from the top side of the mud-wall on the south west comer of the hut. In reply to cross-examination he has denied that he had planted this arm and showed false recovery in collusion with Mujib Master, Kabiluddin, Sanaullah Member and Moyezuddin on account of enmity. It was suggested to this witness that due to enmity someone might keep the arms there. PW 2 was the SI of Police attached to Narsingdi PS at the material time. On 27.8.84 he went to the village Kalait along with accused-appellant Abul Hashem and PW 1 and other Police Forces and PWs 4 and 5. They reached the house of accused appellant at 3.30 PM. In his presence accused-appellant Abul Hashem brought out the pipe-gun, Ext. 1, from the top of the mudwall on the western side of his chouchala mud-walled tin-shed. PW 1 prepared the seizure-list in his presence and other witnesses. He made certain other statements regarding the killing of Fazar Ali with the Ext. 1, which not being admissible in evidence is entirely left out of our discussion. PW 3 MA Jalil, SI also accompanied the police lorce to the house of the accused-appellant and witnessed the accused appellant bringing out the rifle, Ext. 1, He has narrated how the appellant himself brought out the Ext. I from the top of the mud-wall PW. 4 Santosh Kumar has his house one mile from the south west of the house of the appellant. He was present at the bazar near his house together with PW 5 Majid Member. He states that PW 1 came to them in a baby-taxi and took them along with others to the house of accused Hashem Master who admitted that he had arms in his possession. Then the PWs 4 and 5 went to the house of the accused-appellant and witnessed the recovery of the pipe-gun. He has described how the appellant brought out the pipe-gun from the top of the western mud-wall of his chouchala mud-walled tin-shed. He has stated that at first appellant brought out a piece of wood from the upper side of the wall and then a handle of a plough and lastly a country made pipe-gun. PW 1 took it up and showed it to all the witnesses who were at the spot. He has stated that PW 1 prepared the seizure-list and he put his signature on the seizure-list, Ext. 2(1). The cross-examination of this witness reveal that he is a sitting member of Panchduma Union Parishad. He had denied the suggestion that he had beaten and burnt one Asgar by cigarette for selling a tape-recorder and appellant Hashcm Master fined him Taka 1,000.00 for this act of his violence. He has stated that he was sitting in a tea-stall at the bazar when he was called by PW 1. He has stated that Moyezuddin was also present when the recovery of the pipe-gun was made. PW 5 Abdul Majid is also a sitting Member of Panchduma Union Parisand. He has stated that he was taking tea along with PW 4 at the bazar when PWs 1 and 2 approached them and called them to witness the recovery of the pipe-gun. PW 1 told him that appellant Hashem would deliver arms from his possession at his house. Accordingly, PWs 1 and 2 went to the house of appellant Hashem by a baby-taxi. One Moyezuddin was also sitting in the baby-taxi tied up by rope. PWs 4 and 5 went to the house of accused-appellant and reached there at 2-30 and then accused-appellant brought out the pipe-gun with the help of a forked bamboo pole. At first he brought out a piece of wood and then a handle of a plough and lastly, a pipe-gun. PW 1 seized under siezure list which this witness signed. This witness also proved the other signature upon the seizure-list. It was suggested to him that Hashem Master and others in a salish compelled him to return a land to one Fazar and so he deposed falsely against Hashem. PW 6 is the son of Fazar Ali for the murder of whom the PS Case No.15 dated 24.7.84 was started under section 302 BPC. The prosecution maintains that with this gun, Ext.1, the father of this PW was murdered. Now he states that he accompanied the PWs 1 and 2 and the other members of the police force as well as PWs 4 and 5 to the house of the accused appellant Hashem Master. He states that he was present when accused Hashem Master brought out the pipe-gun from the western wall of his west bhiti and-walled hut. He has stated that the accused-appellant first brought out a piece of wood and then a handle of a plough and lastly the pipe-gun which he threw on the floor in presence of this witness and other witnesses. PW 1 took up the pipe-gun and showed it to this witness and others. Then PW 1 prepared a seizure-list. He did not remember when he signed the seizure-list. In reply to cross-examination he stated that his house is about half of a mile from the house of Hashem Master. He deposed before the 10. We got from his cross-examination that there arc four huts in the house of the appellant. PW Siddique Rahman was in the police force who accompanied the PW 1 to the house of accused-appellant. He has stated that he was present when accused Abul Hashem had bought out the pipe-gun with the help of a forked bamboo. He has stated that this took place at 3.30 PM. This witnesses stated that the accused-appellant had killed Fazar Ali by this pipe-gun. In reply to cross-examination he has stated that they were in all 8. He went into a baby-taxi. This witness stated to the 10 that accused-appellant had thrown the pipe-gun on the ground and PW 1 took up it using his handkerchief. PW 8 was also police personnel accompanying the police force making a recovery of the pipe-gun. He has stated that Abul Hashem Master climbed up the mud wall and bought out the pipe-gun with the help of a forked bamboo and threw it on the floor and then he took it up and showed it to all present. PW 9 constable No.103 Omar Ali also was in the police force with PW1. He has stated how Hashem Master brought out the pipe-gun from the top of the western mud-wall of his chouchala mud-walled tin-shed. He has stated that this mud-wall was 8/9 cubits high. He has also stated that by this gun appellant had killed a man. In reply to cross-examination he has stated that he deposed before the IO. He has described how the appellant climbed up and brought out the pipe-gun with the help of a forked bamboo and threw it on the floor. PW 10 Abu Taher constable No.250 was also a member of the police who accompanied PW 1 for making search. He has described how the appellant had brought out the pipe-gun from the top of the western mud-wall which was 8/9 cubits high. PW 11 is no other than PW 1 himself. PW 1 has deposed as PW 11 in the capacity of Investigating Officer. He has stated how he prepared the seizure-list and obtained the signature of witnesses thereon after the pipe-gun was produced by the accused-appellant. It was suggested that the wall from which the pipe-gun was recovered was 12 cubits high and not 8/9 cubits high. 

 12. This is all about the witnesses of the occurrence. It appears that all the evidence of the occurrence except PWs 4 and 5 are police personnel's. The Police personnel's have given a consistent statement as to how the accused-appellant Abul Hashem Master had brought out the pipe-gun from the top of the westen mud-wall of the tin-shed of the appellant. They had given graphic description how the appellant had first brought out the piece of wood and then the handle of a plough and lastly the pipe-gun. They have stated how the accused-appellant had recovered the pipe-gun and dropped it on the floor and how PW 1 took it up using his handkerchief and showed it to all who were present. These police personnels have been elaborately cross-examined and nothing has revealed from their evidence that they were inimically disposed to the accused-appellant. So far as the PWs 4 and 5 are concerned they are the sitting members of the Union Parishad. They have also fully corroborated the prosecution case as to how the pipe-gun was recovered. Two different suggestions were made to PWs 4 and 5 bringing up the solitary instance on account of which these witnesses might be inimically disposed towards the appellant. But both the suggestions are vague. At the time of 342 statement made by the accused-appellant he had not spoken of any enmity of these two witnesses. 

 13. Now there is a definite suggestion to PW 1 that someone out of enmity might have kept the pipe-gun from where it was brought out by the accused-appellant. It was also suggested to him that the mud-wall from the top of which the pipe gun was brought out by the accused-appellant was not 8/9 cubits high but 12 cubits high. These two suggestions made to the PW 1 (PW 11) who is the pilot of the case and the leader of the police force present at the time when the accused-appellant had brought out the pipe-gun go a long way to show that the pipe-gun was recovered from the top of the western wall of the chouchala mud-wall but of the accused-appellant. The evidence on this point is consistent and conclusive. There is no reason why the evidence of the police personnel should be discarded simply because they belonged to police force. They came before the Court and testified to the occurrence. They were fully cross-examined. Their evidence is the evidence within the meaning of section 3 of the Evidence Act. It cannot also be said that these witnesses are interested or inimically disposed towards the accused-appellant. Added to this the fact that suggestions have been made to PW 1 (PW 11) that the pipe-gun might have been planted by the enemy of the appellant and that the wall from which the pipe-gun was recovered was 12 cubits high and not 8/9 cubits high leave no room for doubt that the pipe-gun was recovered by the accused-appellant from the western mud-wall of his but as alleged by the prosecution. 

 14. Now whether the misstatement of the occurrence in the charge-sheet would affect the prosecution case. We have seen that both in the FIR and in the evidence of all the witnesses the time of recovery of the pipe-gun has been given as 3.30 PM. At the time of cross-examination of the accused-appellant under section 342 CrPC time has also been given as 3-30 PM. It is, therefore, clear that the accused-appellant was not prevented from giving a proper defence by the misstatement of the charge-framed by the Court as to the time of the occurrence. Section 225 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is to the effect that "no error in stating either the offence or the particulars required to be stated in the charge, and no omission to state the offence or those particulars, shall be considered at any stage of the case as material, unless the accused was in fact misled by such error or omission, and it has occasioned a failure of justice." Section 535 of the Code is to the effect that no finding or sentence pronounced or passed shall be deemed invalid merely on the ground that no charge was framed, unless, in the opinion of the Court of Appeal or Revision, a failure of justice has, in fact, been occasioned thereby. In the instant case because the FIR and the evidence of the witnesses have clearly brought the exact time of occurrence to the notice of the accused-appellant, a misstatement of the charge as to the time of occurrence cannot mislead the accused- appellant in his defence. The accused-appellant had clearly understood that a charge against him was of possession of an unauthorized arms which he himself had brought out in pursuance of certain statement made by him. Under these circumstances, we find no substance in the argument of the learned Advocate that the trial was vitiated on account of misstatement in the framing of charge regarding the time of occurrence. 

 15. Now coming to the point of search in the instant case, we find that the provision of section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure had been fulfilled. But we find, as submitted by the learned Advocate for the State, fulfillment of the provision of section 103 CrPC was not also required, because the pipe-gun was not recovered by the police personnel on search but it was produced by the accused-appellant himself without requirement for search. The view that the fulfillment of the provision of section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not necessary is supported by the decision in the case of Kochi @ Jishan & on. Vs. The State, reported in 8 BLD, 412 that since the weapon is recovered at the instance of the accused and brought out by him and made over to the police by him there is no scope for search and as such there is no question of application of the procedure of search provided in law. We would endorse this view of the learned Single Bench Judge of the High Court. 

 16. Now we are confined only to the point whether even if the pipe-gun was recovered by the accused-appellant in the manner and at the time and place as alleged by prosecution, the accused-appellant should be found guilty of any offence, section 19 of the Arms Act makes it an offence to have in his possession or under control any arms or ammunition or military stores in contravention of section 14 or 15 ie without any licence. The moot question is whether the accused-appellant was in exclusive possession and control of the pipe-gun in question. In order to bring home this point, the learned Advocate for the appellant has submitted before us certain decisions. Firstly, in the case of Bhuboni Sahu Vs. The King reported in 2 DLR 39 (Privy Council) and in the case of Arshadullilh Vs. the State reported in 21 DLR 684. In these cases it has been held that mere know ledge of the accused that the arms or the ammunition were lying at the spot pointed out by him in the absence of evidence and circumstances to show that he himself kept the same there or that he had exclusive possession over it he cannot be made one liable under section 19F of the Arms Act. In 21 DLR case the appellant with another, namely, one Nurul Islam led the police to a panbaroj near the house of the appellant and pointed out the spot from where a gun had been recovered. Arshadullah made a confessional statement and his conviction was maintained on the ground that he made a confessional statement and also pointed out the spot from where the gun was recovered. But the other appellant was acquitted on the ground that mere knowledge of the location of the spot was not enough because panboraj was an open place accessible to all and equal knowledge of the location of the gun. So the ratio of this decision is that when there is likelihood of others keeping the gun in an open place one should not be convicted merely because he had knowledge of the location of the gun. The other decision cited is in the case of Daud Ali Daud Hossain Vs. the State reported in 27 DLR 251. In this case the arms was recovered from the courtyard of the appellant. It was argued on behalf of the State that recovery from the courtyard of the appellant meant recovery of the gun from the appellant's possession. It was held that this contention if upheld would lead to a dangerous conclusion. This decision only follows the decision of the 21 DLR 684. The other case reported in 41 DLR 525 is the case of Karl Ibrahim @ Ibrahim Vs. the State which also follows 21 DLR 684. Now the sum total of these decisions is that when a weapon is recovered from an open place accessible to others even if it makes a part of the homested of the accused it will not incriminate him. 

 17. Therefore, the question to be disposed of before the Court is whether the appellant had exclusive possession and control of the pipe-gun in question and whether the possession was conscious and with mens rea. It is seen from the evidence on record that the mud-wall from the top of which the gun was recovered was 9 to 10 cubits high. The PW 1 Abdul Majid who led the police force for recovery of the pipe-gun has stated in his cross-examination that "after arriving Hashem Master did not disclose the place where he kept the arm. First he searched one of his other huts but he did not get anything there. Then again he started search and after 5n minutes he brought out the arm from the top of the mud wall with the help of a pronged bamboo pole" Again in reply to cross-examination he has stated that one could push his arm from outside to top of the mud-wall. This statement of PW 1 tends to show that the accused was not sure where the pipe-gun was kept and that he had to search one of his other huts. In fact, he made search for 5/7 minutes before he could bring out the gun in question. A doubt arises that the accused-appellant was not aware where the gun was kept. The spot from where the arm was recovered was also accessible from outside so that one could push his arm outside of the mud-wall. It appears that the recovery was made in pursuance of the initial interrogation of Maijuddin and Mafiuddin was also in the search party. Maijuddin has not been made an accused in this case nor a witness. It cannot be ruled out that the cut rifle might have been planted by one of the enemies of this accused-appellant as suggested to the witnesses of the defence. It may also be a machination on the part of Maizuddin who made the first disclosure. Be that as it may, one cannot be very certain that the accused himself had kept the gun from where he had recovered the same. If the accused had been very certain about the location of the cut pipe-gun he would not have searched other places of his house and he would not have taken 5/7 minutes to find out the pipe-gun. In the above circumstances, we find that the appellant should get the benefit of doubt.
